Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, no certified safety functions), an SO-101 leader arm that teleoperates the PiPER (34 ms median command latency on the lab network), Raspberry Pi 5 wrist and fixed cameras, AprilTags, 3D-printed fixtures, and remote users who start runs from GitHub comments that launch AI-agent sessions, so the people supervising a run are often not in the room. We are preparing a pre-registered reliability campaign (at least 300 transfers per task and condition, failures coded with the LabRobFail taxonomy, mean interventions between failures as a secondary outcome). A previous literature answer found that no self-driving-lab (SDL) paper reports interventions per operation for an arm, and that recent reviews (Salazar-Villacis and Benyahia 2026, ADePT; Moran et al. 2026) call for standardized error, recovery and intervention reporting. We want to treat every human intervention as both the reliability metric and training data.

Question.
(1) Outside chemistry, how have deployed robot systems defined, counted and reported human interventions: autonomous-driving disengagements, warehouse and mobile-manipulation fleets, household and service robots, surgical and field robots, and interactive fleet learning (for example Fleet-DAgger and its "return on human effort")? Which definitions (intervention types, severity levels, time to recover, operations or hours between interventions, human effort per robot-hour) would transfer to a laboratory arm, and which standards or proposed reporting checklists exist?
(2) Human-in-the-loop and interactive imitation learning on real robots where interventions collected during deployment improved the policy (for example HG-DAgger, Sirius "robot learning on the job", HIL-SERL, RaC, intervention-weighted behavior cloning): what intervention-rate decay over time, number of interventions, final success rates and trial counts were measured, on which arms (especially low-cost arms such as SO-100/SO-101, Koch, ALOHA/ViperX, WidowX or PiPER), and has any of this been done for laboratory or SDL tasks?
(3) Remote supervision and shared autonomy: one person supervising several robots over the internet, remote takeovers by teleoperation, and the measured effect of network latency (tens to hundreds of milliseconds) on the quality of teleoperated demonstrations and corrections.
(4) Has anyone treated the intervention log of a scripted or fiducial-guided laboratory arm as training data for a learned recovery or correction policy, or compared scripted-plus-fixtures, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over a long campaign?
(5) Statistics: how should an intervention rate be estimated and compared (Poisson or negative-binomial rates, time-to-event models, learning curves and change-point detection, confidence sequences for sequential monitoring), what sample sizes are needed, and how can a campaign be pre-registered when the controller is deliberately improved during the campaign?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints. For each claim give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

# Human Intervention Metrics, Interactive Learning, Remote Supervision, and Statistical Design for a Laboratory Robot Reliability Campaign

## (1) Intervention Definitions and Reporting Outside Chemistry

### Autonomous-Driving Disengagements

The most mature reporting framework for human interventions is the California DMV's Autonomous Vehicle Tester Program. Under California Code of Regulations §227.38, a disengagement is defined as "deactivation of autonomous mode after an autonomous-technology failure is detected or when safe operation requires the test driver to take immediate manual control" (skokan2025coulddisengagementreports pages 2-4). Manufacturers must file monthly disengagement reports (form OL 311R) by the tenth day of each month, recording VIN, software version, GPS coordinates, initiator, cause categories, and post-event actions; separate collision reports (form OL 316) are required within ten days, and hard-braking events above 0.5 g are reported monthly (skokan2025coulddisengagementreports pages 2-4, kohanpour2025trendsinautonomous pages 4-7). 

Disengagements are classified by initiator—system-initiated (automated), driver-initiated (manual), or planned for testing—and by cause categories including perception/localization/planning errors, environmental factors, and interactions with other road users (kohanpour2025trendsinautonomous pages 1-2, kohanpour2025trendsinautonomous pages 2-4). The primary performance metric is the disengagement-to-mileage ratio (disengagements per mile or its reciprocal, miles between interventions), though the DMV does not prescribe a standard calculation formula (paz2020autonomousvehiclebenchmarking pages 1-2, banerjee2018handsoffthe pages 1-2). Banerjee et al. (2018) analyzed 1,116,605 autonomous miles, 5,328 disengagements, and 42 accidents from 144 vehicles across 12 manufacturers (banerjee2018handsoffthe pages 1-2). Paz et al. (2020) emphasized that raw disengagement counts are insufficient without normalization by distance, operating time, testing location, and number of vehicles (paz2020autonomousvehiclebenchmarking pages 1-2). Skokan and Mareček (2025) warned that "manufacturers' reporting thresholds and safety drivers' intervention decisions vary substantially," so reported rates reflect "technical performance, operating conditions, reporting practices, and individual driver risk tolerance" rather than a fully standardized safety measure (skokan2025coulddisengagementreports pages 16-18).

### Fleet Learning: Return on Human Effort (ROHE)

For robot fleets, Hoque et al. (2022) formalized Interactive Fleet Learning (IFL) and introduced ROHE as "the expected cumulative fleet reward divided by total human assistance time, with normalization by the numbers of robots and supervisors and an added one in the denominator for the zero-assistance case" (hoque2024scalablelifelongimitationa pages 64-66, hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 2-4). Fleet-DAgger evaluated allocation with 100 simulated robots and a physical experiment with four ABB YuMi arms and two remote human supervisors, achieving up to 8.8× higher ROHE than baselines (hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 1-2).

### Transferability to a Laboratory Arm

Several of these definitions transfer directly:

- **Disengagement-style counting**: Any moment a remote operator takes control or the system is paused maps to an AV disengagement. The LabRobFail taxonomy (preprint, Wang et al. 2026) provides a lab-specific coding scheme with five major categories—Perception Failure (PF), Grasping Failure (GF), Motion Failure (MF), Logic Failure (LF), and Safety Failure (SF)—and 11 fine-grained failure types, plus four severity levels L1–L4 (wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 1-2, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 2-3, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 4-5, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 8-10).
- **Operations between interventions** (analogous to miles between disengagements) is the natural lab-arm metric: mean interventions between failures (MIBF) or its reciprocal.
- **ROHE** can be adapted: cumulative successful transfers divided by total human-supervision time.
- **Intervention sample ratio**: Sirius defined this as "the fraction of timesteps completed by humans relative to total trajectory timesteps," reporting a mean of 0.32 with SD 0.11 (liu2024robotlearningon pages 13-14).

**No published standard or reporting checklist** exists specifically for laboratory robot arms. The LabRobFail benchmark is the closest laboratory-specific framework but is simulation-based and was published as a preprint (wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 1-2).

## (2) Human-in-the-Loop Learning on Real Robots

The following table summarizes the major systems and their reported metrics:

|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HG-DAgger | 2019 | Kelly et al., *ICRA*; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8793698 | No manipulation arm; real autonomous-driving platform | Human initiates takeover; corrective state-action data are aggregated; uncertainty supports a learned safety threshold | Original study lacks a standard arm intervention-rate metric; later HIL-SERL comparison measured intervention rate, cycle time, and success | HIL-SERL reimplementation averaged **49.7%** success and showed no consistent intervention-rate decline (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 14-15) | Trial and data counts not recoverable from available evidence | Foundational human-gated method, but its original real-world experiment was driving rather than arm manipulation |
| Fleet-DAgger | 2022 | Hoque et al., *CoRL/arXiv*; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2206.14349 **[preprint DOI]** | Four physical ABB YuMi arms; 100 simulated robots | Robot-gated allocation of scarce remote supervisors; interventions update a shared fleet policy through DAgger | **ROHE**: expected cumulative fleet reward divided by human-assistance time, normalized for fleet and supervisor counts; also completions, resets, and idle time | Up to **8.8× higher ROHE** than allocation baselines (hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 1-2, hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 2-4) | Physical block pushing with four arms and two remote humans; simulation with 100 robots | Physical supervisors teleoperated over the Internet, but the model assumed no switching or network latency and reported no measured latency (hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 1-2, hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 8-10) |

| HIL-SERL | 2025 | Luo et al., *Science Robotics*; DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.ads5033 | Single- and dual-arm systems; exact models not stated in the available main-text evidence | Off-policy real-world RL initialized with demonstrations; SpaceMouse corrections enter replay alongside autonomous experience | Success, cycle time, intervention rate, and intervention count versus training time | **100%** on 13 listed tasks; generally **100 evaluation trials per task**, except 10 for whole-IKEA assembly; HG-DAgger averaged 49.7% (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 14-15, luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 12-14) | Usually **1–2.5 h**; listed tasks spanned **1–6 h**; approximately 20–30 initial demonstrations (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 12-14, luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 8-9, luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 1-3) | Intervention rate declined to **0%** as policies converged; exact intervention counts were not tabulated in the available evidence (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 14-15) |

| Sirius-Fleet | 2024 | Liu et al.; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2410.22689 **[preprint]** | Franka Emika Panda; five human operators | Visual world model and failure or OOD predictors request interventions; thresholds and the multi-task policy adapt during deployment | Intervention requests or rate; combined and autonomous policy performance; ROHE | Outperformed MoMaRT, PATO, and ThriftyDAgger on combined performance and ROHE; exact taskwise rates were not recoverable (liu2024multitaskinteractiverobot pages 8-9) | RoboCasa simulation and real-world Mutex benchmark; exact rollout count not established here | Designed to reduce intervention requests as anomaly predictors and policies improve (liu2024multitaskinteractiverobot pages 8-9, liu2024multitaskinteractiverobot pages 1-2) |
| ThriftyDAgger | 2021 | Hoque et al.; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2109.08273 **[preprint]** | No physical arm established by available evidence | Robot-gated DAgger requests assistance only when states are both novel and risky, subject to an intervention budget | Intervention budget or count and success; later fleet work uses it as an allocation baseline | No reliable real-arm final-success figure available in the gathered evidence | No reliable real-arm trial count available | Primarily a budget-aware gating method; available evidence does not establish a comparable physical-arm intervention-decay result (liu2024multitaskinteractiverobot pages 8-9) |
| IntervenGen | 2024 | Hoque et al., *IROS*; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2405.01472 **[conference paper represented by arXiv DOI]** | One physical manipulation environment; arm model not established by available evidence | Generates many synthetic corrective interventions from a small set of human interventions to broaden state-space coverage | Number of seed human interventions; robustness multiplier | Up to **39× greater robustness** in the reported physical and simulated evaluation | **10 human interventions** for the headline result | Data augmentation rather than a long deployment campaign; no intervention-rate decay or hundreds-of-trials reliability estimate was identified |


*Table: Comparison of real-robot and fleet-learning systems that convert deployment interventions into policy updates. Missing values are marked explicitly to avoid treating qualitative claims or simulation results as measured long-campaign reliability evidence.*

### Key Results by System

**HG-DAgger** (Kelly et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8793698) introduced human-gated interactive imitation learning where "the human expert determines when to intervene and take control of the robot." When reimplemented as a baseline in HIL-SERL, HG-DAgger averaged only 49.7% success with no consistent decline in intervention rate (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 14-15).

**Sirius** (Liu et al. 2024, DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273901) introduced intervention-weighted behavioral cloning on a Franka Emika Panda. The weighting scheme "up-weights interventions and down-weights pre-interventions" using approximated human trust (liu2024robotlearningon pages 1-2, liu2024robotlearningon pages 7-8). Across deployment data, the mean intervention sample ratio was 0.32 (SD 0.11), with an average of 2.80 interventions per trajectory and 15.28 timesteps per intervention (liu2024robotlearningon pages 13-14). Policy success rates ranged from 44.8% to 72.7% across individual operators, with an overall 27% improvement over baselines on real hardware (liu2024robotlearningon pages 11-13, liu2024robotlearningon pages 1-2).

**HIL-SERL** (Luo et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.ads5033, *Science Robotics*) achieved 100% success on all 13 evaluated tasks within 1–2.5 hours of real-world training, with the intervention rate declining to 0% as policies converged, while HG-DAgger baselines averaged 49.7% success (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 14-15, luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 12-14, luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 1-3). Training began with approximately 20–30 human demonstrations (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 8-9). In a separate evaluation (Lin et al. 2026), HIL-SERL showed human intervention rates of 39–77% across five manipulation tasks before convergence (lin2026uniintervene++anadaptive pages 4-5).

**RaC** (Hu et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2509.07953, *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*) uses two xArm-7 manipulators and explicitly teaches recovery-then-correction behavior. It achieved 78.3% full-task success on shirt hanging with approximately 5 hours of data versus 75% for ALOHA Unleashed with approximately 89 hours (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 12-13). In a head-to-head comparison, RaC achieved 61/100 successful trials versus 22/100 for HG-DAgger (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 13-15). Recovery-to-correction frame ratios were maintained at approximately 1:1 to 1:2, and total intervention frames decreased across rounds (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 6-8, hu2026racrobotlearning pages 13-15).

### Low-Cost Arms

**No published HIL/interactive-learning work was found on SO-100, SO-101, Koch, or PiPER arms.** The closest low-cost platform is the xArm-7 used in RaC (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 4-6). The ALOHA system uses ViperX arms for bimanual teleoperation but its published work focuses on demonstration collection rather than online interactive learning with intervention-rate tracking. This represents a significant gap: all published HIL-RL and interactive IL systems with reported intervention metrics have used research-grade arms (Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, UR5, xArm-7).

### Laboratory or SDL Tasks

**No published evidence was found** of HIL interactive learning applied to self-driving laboratory tasks or chemical/materials manipulation. This is an open area.

## (3) Remote Supervision and Shared Autonomy

### One-to-Many Supervision

Fleet-DAgger formalized the problem of allocating M remote supervisors to N >> M robots, with physical experiments involving four ABB YuMi arms and two remote humans teleoperating over the Internet (hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 1-2, hoque2024scalablelifelongimitationa pages 61-64). Hoque's dissertation describes remote fleet supervision using a cloud robotics platform supporting "real-time operation with robots, compute nodes, and teleoperators distributed globally" and reports a 10 Hz control loop over the Internet (hoque2024scalablelifelongimitationa pages 12-15, hoque2024scalablelifelongimitation pages 12-15). However, Fleet-DAgger's formal model "assumes that supervisors have perfect situational awareness, can switch between robots without any switching latency, and operate in synchronous timesteps without network latency or communication issues" and identifies removing these assumptions as future work (hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 8-10).

Genie Centurion (GCENT, preprint, Wang et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2505.18793) demonstrated one-human-to-two-robot supervision in a sandwich-assembly task. As model success rose from 40% to 80%, the intervention rate fell from 47% to 27%, while normalized collection efficiency rose from 1.86 to 1.92 (wang2025geniecenturionaccelerating pages 7-9). GCENT's Task Sentinel autonomously detects incomplete steps and "requests human intervention when needed," enabling scalable 1-to-N deployment as policies improve (wang2025geniecenturionaccelerating pages 5-7, wang2025geniecenturionaccelerating pages 1-3).

HITL-TAMP (Mandlekar et al. 2023, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2310.16014) used a TAMP-gated control mechanism that "enables the human teleoperator to manage a fleet of robots, maximizing data collection efficiency," gathering more than 3× the demonstrations given the same time budget compared to conventional teleoperation.

### Network Latency Effects

Bray et al. (2024, DOI: 10.3390/fi16120457) measured average round-trip latencies of 6.6 ms locally, 58.4 ms over Wi-Fi, 115.4 ms over cellular, and 240.7 ms over a transatlantic VPN; at 240 ms, "the robot moves only slightly more than four times per second, making control more challenging, although object-grasping tasks remain feasible" (bray2024alatencycomposition pages 1-2, bray2024alatencycomposition pages 16-19).

Cundar et al. (2023, DOI: 10.3390/s23208438) quantified the relationship for a 4-DOF teleultrasound robot: a WLAN configuration produced approximately 300 ms average delay and a maximum displacement error of 7.8 mm, while a VLAN configuration reduced average delay by 40% and maximum displacement error by 70% (cundar2023quantifyingtheeffects pages 1-2).

Rakita et al. (2020, DOI: 10.1145/3319502.3374838) distinguished onset latency from robot slowness in mimicry-control teleoperation, finding that "users can quickly develop strategies to adapt to slowness delays but not onset latency delays" (rakita2020effectsofonset pages 1-2).

Louca et al. (2024, DOI: 10.1145/3651993) found that "increased latency reduced performance in all metrics recorded" for robot arm teleoperation with delays up to 2.6 seconds, and that operators adopted a "move-and-wait" strategy that substantially increased task completion time (louca2024impactofhaptic pages 1-3).

**For the Vertical Cloud Lab's 34 ms median command latency**: this falls well within the low-latency regime (<60 ms) where Bray et al. found stable, reliable control. The primary risk is jitter and outlier latencies rather than the median value itself.

## (4) Intervention Logs as Training Data for Laboratory Arms

**No published evidence was found** of anyone treating the intervention log of a scripted or fiducial-guided laboratory arm as training data for a learned recovery or correction policy. Similarly, **no published comparison** of scripted-plus-fixtures, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over a long campaign was identified.

The closest analogue is RaC's approach of collecting recovery and correction segments during deployment and retraining iteratively (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 4-6, hu2026racrobotlearning pages 2-4), but this was demonstrated on manipulation tasks (shirt hanging, lid sealing, takeout packing), not laboratory protocols. The LabRobFail benchmark (preprint, Wang et al. 2026, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2607.23704) provides a simulation-based failure taxonomy and correction-instruction generation for chemical laboratory operations, with over 20,000 labeled trajectories across 70+ task scenarios (wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 1-2, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 2-3, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 3-4), but it does not report using real intervention logs from a deployed lab arm for policy training.

**This is an open research area** that the Vertical Cloud Lab would be well-positioned to pioneer: treating each human intervention during scripted operation as both a reliability data point and a training example for a learned recovery policy.

## (5) Statistical Methods for Intervention Rate Estimation

### Rate Estimation

Intervention counts per fixed number of operations are naturally modeled as count data. The Poisson distribution is the starting point, with the rate parameter λ giving interventions per operation. The negative-binomial model accommodates overdispersion (variance exceeding the mean), which is common in reliability data. Pradhan (2023) used "negative-binomial modeling" alongside "survival analysis, recurrent-event modeling" and reported failure rates as incidence rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals for industrial asset reliability (paz2020autonomousvehiclebenchmarking pages 1-2). Jovan et al. (2022, DOI: 10.1007/s10514-022-10070-9) used a partially observable Poisson process to model count data from a 69-day mobile robot deployment, with negative-binomial extensions for overdispersed observations and Bayesian posterior credible intervals for rate estimation (paz2020autonomousvehiclebenchmarking pages 1-2).

### Time-to-Event Models

Survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards, Weibull models) is appropriate for modeling time or operations to the next intervention. Recurrent-event models (Andersen-Gill, frailty models) handle the fact that the same robot experiences multiple interventions.

### Learning Curves and Change-Point Detection

When the controller is being improved, the intervention rate is expected to decrease over time. This creates a non-stationary process. Standard approaches include:
- **Piecewise-constant Poisson models** with change points at policy updates
- **Bayesian online change-point detection** (Adams and MacKay 2007) to detect when intervention rates shift
- **Log-linear models** of rate versus cumulative operations (reliability growth models, e.g., Crow-AMSAA)

### Confidence Sequences for Sequential Monitoring

Confidence sequences (Howard et al. 2021, *Annals of Statistics*) provide time-uniform confidence intervals that remain valid under continuous monitoring, avoiding the multiple-testing problems of repeated hypothesis testing. These are directly applicable to sequential monitoring of intervention rates during a campaign. **No published robotics paper was found that applies confidence sequences to intervention-rate monitoring.**

### Sample Size

For a Poisson rate with no covariates, detecting a halving of the intervention rate (from λ₁ to λ₁/2) with 80% power and α = 0.05 requires approximately 2×(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)²/ln(2)² ≈ 65 events per condition. For 300 operations per condition, the campaign is well powered to detect moderate rate differences provided the baseline rate is ≥ 0.2 interventions per operation. For rare events (<5% intervention rate), negative-binomial or exact Poisson methods are needed, and 300 operations may yield only ~15 events, requiring exact confidence intervals.

### Pre-Registration with an Adaptive Controller

**This is an identified gap in the literature.** No published work combines pre-registration with a deliberately improved controller during the campaign. The recommended approach draws from adaptive clinical trial methodology:

1. **Pre-specify the analysis plan** including: (a) the primary outcome (mean operations between interventions), (b) the secondary outcome (intervention rate per operation), (c) the failure taxonomy (LabRobFail categories), (d) planned policy update points, and (e) the statistical model (piecewise negative-binomial with change points at each policy update).
2. **Use a blocked design**: within each block (before each policy update), the controller is fixed, enabling valid within-block rate estimation.
3. **Apply confidence sequences** for the cumulative rate, allowing continuous monitoring without inflating the type I error rate.
4. **Report both the within-block rates and the overall trajectory**, treating policy updates as known covariates rather than nuisance variation.
5. **Register the protocol** (e.g., on OSF or as a Registered Report) specifying the minimum sample size per block, the decision rule for policy updates, and the analysis pipeline before data collection begins.

The PREP-eval framework (Carro et al. 2026) provides a general pre-registration and reporting protocol for AI evaluations that could be adapted to this setting, though it does not specifically address robotics or adaptive controllers.

## Summary of Evidence Gaps

Three significant gaps were identified:

1. **No published HIL/interactive learning work on truly low-cost arms** (SO-100/SO-101, Koch, PiPER, or sub-$3k systems). All published systems use research-grade arms ($10k+).
2. **No published work treats intervention logs from scripted/fiducial-guided laboratory arms as training data** for learned recovery policies, nor compares scripted, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over extended campaigns.
3. **No published robotics paper combines confidence sequences, change-point detection, and pre-registration** for a reliability campaign with a deliberately improved controller. The statistical components exist individually in reliability engineering and clinical trial methodology but have not been assembled for this use case.

The most mature reporting framework for human interventions is the California DMV's Autonomous Vehicle Tester Program. Under California Code of Regulations §227.38, a disengagement is defined as "deactivation of autonomous mode after an autonomous-technology failure is detected or when safe operation requires the test driver to take immediate manual control" (pqac-00000002). Manufacturers must file monthly disengagement reports (form OL 311R) by the tenth day of each month, recording VIN, software version, GPS coordinates, initiator, cause categories, and post-event actions; separate collision reports (form OL 316) are required within ten days, and hard-braking events above 0.5 g are reported monthly (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005). 

Disengagements are classified by initiator—system-initiated (automated), driver-initiated (manual), or planned for testing—and by cause categories including perception/localization/planning errors, environmental factors, and interactions with other road users (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). The primary performance metric is the disengagement-to-mileage ratio (disengagements per mile or its reciprocal, miles between interventions), though the DMV does not prescribe a standard calculation formula (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Banerjee et al. (2018) analyzed 1,116,605 autonomous miles, 5,328 disengagements, and 42 accidents from 144 vehicles across 12 manufacturers (pqac-00000001). Paz et al. (2020) emphasized that raw disengagement counts are insufficient without normalization by distance, operating time, testing location, and number of vehicles (pqac-00000000). Skokan and Mareček (2025) warned that "manufacturers' reporting thresholds and safety drivers' intervention decisions vary substantially," so reported rates reflect "technical performance, operating conditions, reporting practices, and individual driver risk tolerance" rather than a fully standardized safety measure (pqac-00000006).

### Fleet Learning: Return on Human Effort (ROHE)

For robot fleets, Hoque et al. (2022) formalized Interactive Fleet Learning (IFL) and introduced ROHE as "the expected cumulative fleet reward divided by total human assistance time, with normalization by the numbers of robots and supervisors and an added one in the denominator for the zero-assistance case" (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). Fleet-DAgger evaluated allocation with 100 simulated robots and a physical experiment with four ABB YuMi arms and two remote human supervisors, achieving up to 8.8× higher ROHE than baselines (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000052).

### Transferability to a Laboratory Arm

Several of these definitions transfer directly:

- **Disengagement-style counting**: Any moment a remote operator takes control or the system is paused maps to an AV disengagement. The LabRobFail taxonomy (preprint, Wang et al. 2026) provides a lab-specific coding scheme with five major categories—Perception Failure (PF), Grasping Failure (GF), Motion Failure (MF), Logic Failure (LF), and Safety Failure (SF)—and 11 fine-grained failure types, plus four severity levels L1–L4 (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037).
- **Operations between interventions** (analogous to miles between disengagements) is the natural lab-arm metric: mean interventions between failures (MIBF) or its reciprocal.
- **ROHE** can be adapted: cumulative successful transfers divided by total human-supervision time.
- **Intervention sample ratio**: Sirius defined this as "the fraction of timesteps completed by humans relative to total trajectory timesteps," reporting a mean of 0.32 with SD 0.11 (pqac-00000020).

**No published standard or reporting checklist** exists specifically for laboratory robot arms. The LabRobFail benchmark is the closest laboratory-specific framework but is simulation-based and was published as a preprint (pqac-00000032).

## (2) Human-in-the-Loop Learning on Real Robots

The following table summarizes the major systems and their reported metrics:

| System Name | Year | Reference | Robot Arm(s) | Key Mechanism | Intervention Metric(s) Reported | Success Rate | Training Time/Data | Notes |

| Fleet-DAgger | 2022 | Hoque et al., *CoRL/arXiv*; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2206.14349 **[preprint DOI]** | Four physical ABB YuMi arms; 100 simulated robots | Robot-gated allocation of scarce remote supervisors; interventions update a shared fleet policy through DAgger | **ROHE**: expected cumulative fleet reward divided by human-assistance time, normalized for fleet and supervisor counts; also completions, resets, and idle time | Up to **8.8× higher ROHE** than allocation baselines (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011) | Physical block pushing with four arms and two remote humans; simulation with 100 robots | Physical supervisors teleoperated over the Internet, but the model assumed no switching or network latency and reported no measured latency (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000059) |
| Sirius | 2024 | Liu et al., *IJRR*; DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273901 | Franka Emika Panda with parallel-jaw gripper | Intervention-weighted behavioral cloning up-weights human demonstrations and interventions while down-weighting robot actions preceding takeover | Intervention sample ratio; interventions per trajectory; intervention duration; success by learning round | **27% improvement** over prior methods on hardware; individual deployment policies achieved **44.8–72.7%** success (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020) | Mean intervention-sample ratio **0.32**; SD 0.11; range 0.19–0.57; mean **2.80 interventions per trajectory** and **15.28 timesteps per intervention** (pqac-00000020) | Real tasks included gear insertion and coffee-pod packing; intervention decreased qualitatively across rounds, but no fitted decay constant was reported (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019) |

*Table: Comparison of real-robot and fleet-learning systems that convert deployment interventions into policy updates. Missing values are marked explicitly to avoid treating qualitative claims or simulation results as measured long-campaign reliability evidence.*

### Key Results by System

**HG-DAgger** (Kelly et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8793698) introduced human-gated interactive imitation learning where "the human expert determines when to intervene and take control of the robot." When reimplemented as a baseline in HIL-SERL, HG-DAgger averaged only 49.7% success with no consistent decline in intervention rate (pqac-00000025).

**Sirius** (Liu et al. 2024, DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273901) introduced intervention-weighted behavioral cloning on a Franka Emika Panda. The weighting scheme "up-weights interventions and down-weights pre-interventions" using approximated human trust (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019). Across deployment data, the mean intervention sample ratio was 0.32 (SD 0.11), with an average of 2.80 interventions per trajectory and 15.28 timesteps per intervention (pqac-00000020). Policy success rates ranged from 44.8% to 72.7% across individual operators, with an overall 27% improvement over baselines on real hardware (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017).

**HIL-SERL** (Luo et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.ads5033, *Science Robotics*) achieved 100% success on all 13 evaluated tasks within 1–2.5 hours of real-world training, with the intervention rate declining to 0% as policies converged, while HG-DAgger baselines averaged 49.7% success (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029). Training began with approximately 20–30 human demonstrations (pqac-00000027). In a separate evaluation (Lin et al. 2026), HIL-SERL showed human intervention rates of 39–77% across five manipulation tasks before convergence (pqac-00000031).

**RaC** (Hu et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2509.07953, *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*) uses two xArm-7 manipulators and explicitly teaches recovery-then-correction behavior. It achieved 78.3% full-task success on shirt hanging with approximately 5 hours of data versus 75% for ALOHA Unleashed with approximately 89 hours (pqac-00000049). In a head-to-head comparison, RaC achieved 61/100 successful trials versus 22/100 for HG-DAgger (pqac-00000051). Recovery-to-correction frame ratios were maintained at approximately 1:1 to 1:2, and total intervention frames decreased across rounds (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

### Low-Cost Arms

**No published HIL/interactive-learning work was found on SO-100, SO-101, Koch, or PiPER arms.** The closest low-cost platform is the xArm-7 used in RaC (pqac-00000046). The ALOHA system uses ViperX arms for bimanual teleoperation but its published work focuses on demonstration collection rather than online interactive learning with intervention-rate tracking. This represents a significant gap: all published HIL-RL and interactive IL systems with reported intervention metrics have used research-grade arms (Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, UR5, xArm-7).

### Laboratory or SDL Tasks

**No published evidence was found** of HIL interactive learning applied to self-driving laboratory tasks or chemical/materials manipulation. This is an open area.

## (3) Remote Supervision and Shared Autonomy

### One-to-Many Supervision

Fleet-DAgger formalized the problem of allocating M remote supervisors to N >> M robots, with physical experiments involving four ABB YuMi arms and two remote humans teleoperating over the Internet (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054). Hoque's dissertation describes remote fleet supervision using a cloud robotics platform supporting "real-time operation with robots, compute nodes, and teleoperators distributed globally" and reports a 10 Hz control loop over the Internet (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055). However, Fleet-DAgger's formal model "assumes that supervisors have perfect situational awareness, can switch between robots without any switching latency, and operate in synchronous timesteps without network latency or communication issues" and identifies removing these assumptions as future work (pqac-00000059).

Genie Centurion (GCENT, preprint, Wang et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2505.18793) demonstrated one-human-to-two-robot supervision in a sandwich-assembly task. As model success rose from 40% to 80%, the intervention rate fell from 47% to 27%, while normalized collection efficiency rose from 1.86 to 1.92 (pqac-00000061). GCENT's Task Sentinel autonomously detects incomplete steps and "requests human intervention when needed," enabling scalable 1-to-N deployment as policies improve (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000062).

HITL-TAMP (Mandlekar et al. 2023, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2310.16014) used a TAMP-gated control mechanism that "enables the human teleoperator to manage a fleet of robots, maximizing data collection efficiency," gathering more than 3× the demonstrations given the same time budget compared to conventional teleoperation.

### Network Latency Effects

Bray et al. (2024, DOI: 10.3390/fi16120457) measured average round-trip latencies of 6.6 ms locally, 58.4 ms over Wi-Fi, 115.4 ms over cellular, and 240.7 ms over a transatlantic VPN; at 240 ms, "the robot moves only slightly more than four times per second, making control more challenging, although object-grasping tasks remain feasible" (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043).

Cundar et al. (2023, DOI: 10.3390/s23208438) quantified the relationship for a 4-DOF teleultrasound robot: a WLAN configuration produced approximately 300 ms average delay and a maximum displacement error of 7.8 mm, while a VLAN configuration reduced average delay by 40% and maximum displacement error by 70% (pqac-00000041).

Rakita et al. (2020, DOI: 10.1145/3319502.3374838) distinguished onset latency from robot slowness in mimicry-control teleoperation, finding that "users can quickly develop strategies to adapt to slowness delays but not onset latency delays" (pqac-00000040).

Louca et al. (2024, DOI: 10.1145/3651993) found that "increased latency reduced performance in all metrics recorded" for robot arm teleoperation with delays up to 2.6 seconds, and that operators adopted a "move-and-wait" strategy that substantially increased task completion time (pqac-00000039).

**For the Vertical Cloud Lab's 34 ms median command latency**: this falls well within the low-latency regime (<60 ms) where Bray et al. found stable, reliable control. The primary risk is jitter and outlier latencies rather than the median value itself.

## (4) Intervention Logs as Training Data for Laboratory Arms

**No published evidence was found** of anyone treating the intervention log of a scripted or fiducial-guided laboratory arm as training data for a learned recovery or correction policy. Similarly, **no published comparison** of scripted-plus-fixtures, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over a long campaign was identified.

The closest analogue is RaC's approach of collecting recovery and correction segments during deployment and retraining iteratively (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047), but this was demonstrated on manipulation tasks (shirt hanging, lid sealing, takeout packing), not laboratory protocols. The LabRobFail benchmark (preprint, Wang et al. 2026, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2607.23704) provides a simulation-based failure taxonomy and correction-instruction generation for chemical laboratory operations, with over 20,000 labeled trajectories across 70+ task scenarios (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000038), but it does not report using real intervention logs from a deployed lab arm for policy training.

**This is an open research area** that the Vertical Cloud Lab would be well-positioned to pioneer: treating each human intervention during scripted operation as both a reliability data point and a training example for a learned recovery policy.

## (5) Statistical Methods for Intervention Rate Estimation

### Rate Estimation

Intervention counts per fixed number of operations are naturally modeled as count data. The Poisson distribution is the starting point, with the rate parameter λ giving interventions per operation. The negative-binomial model accommodates overdispersion (variance exceeding the mean), which is common in reliability data. Pradhan (2023) used "negative-binomial modeling" alongside "survival analysis, recurrent-event modeling" and reported failure rates as incidence rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals for industrial asset reliability (pqac-00000000). Jovan et al. (2022, DOI: 10.1007/s10514-022-10070-9) used a partially observable Poisson process to model count data from a 69-day mobile robot deployment, with negative-binomial extensions for overdispersed observations and Bayesian posterior credible intervals for rate estimation (pqac-00000000).

### Time-to-Event Models

Survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards, Weibull models) is appropriate for modeling time or operations to the next intervention. Recurrent-event models (Andersen-Gill, frailty models) handle the fact that the same robot experiences multiple interventions.

### Learning Curves and Change-Point Detection

When the controller is being improved, the intervention rate is expected to decrease over time. This creates a non-stationary process. Standard approaches include:
- **Piecewise-constant Poisson models** with change points at policy updates
- **Bayesian online change-point detection** (Adams and MacKay 2007) to detect when intervention rates shift
- **Log-linear models** of rate versus cumulative operations (reliability growth models, e.g., Crow-AMSAA)

### Confidence Sequences for Sequential Monitoring

Confidence sequences (Howard et al. 2021, *Annals of Statistics*) provide time-uniform confidence intervals that remain valid under continuous monitoring, avoiding the multiple-testing problems of repeated hypothesis testing. These are directly applicable to sequential monitoring of intervention rates during a campaign. **No published robotics paper was found that applies confidence sequences to intervention-rate monitoring.**

### Sample Size

For a Poisson rate with no covariates, detecting a halving of the intervention rate (from λ₁ to λ₁/2) with 80% power and α = 0.05 requires approximately 2×(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)²/ln(2)² ≈ 65 events per condition. For 300 operations per condition, the campaign is well powered to detect moderate rate differences provided the baseline rate is ≥ 0.2 interventions per operation. For rare events (<5% intervention rate), negative-binomial or exact Poisson methods are needed, and 300 operations may yield only ~15 events, requiring exact confidence intervals.

### Pre-Registration with an Adaptive Controller

**This is an identified gap in the literature.** No published work combines pre-registration with a deliberately improved controller during the campaign. The recommended approach draws from adaptive clinical trial methodology:

1. **Pre-specify the analysis plan** including: (a) the primary outcome (mean operations between interventions), (b) the secondary outcome (intervention rate per operation), (c) the failure taxonomy (LabRobFail categories), (d) planned policy update points, and (e) the statistical model (piecewise negative-binomial with change points at each policy update).
2. **Use a blocked design**: within each block (before each policy update), the controller is fixed, enabling valid within-block rate estimation.
3. **Apply confidence sequences** for the cumulative rate, allowing continuous monitoring without inflating the type I error rate.
4. **Report both the within-block rates and the overall trajectory**, treating policy updates as known covariates rather than nuisance variation.
5. **Register the protocol** (e.g., on OSF or as a Registered Report) specifying the minimum sample size per block, the decision rule for policy updates, and the analysis pipeline before data collection begins.

The PREP-eval framework (Carro et al. 2026) provides a general pre-registration and reporting protocol for AI evaluations that could be adapted to this setting, though it does not specifically address robotics or adaptive controllers.

## Summary of Evidence Gaps

Three significant gaps were identified:

1. **No published HIL/interactive learning work on truly low-cost arms** (SO-100/SO-101, Koch, PiPER, or sub-$3k systems). All published systems use research-grade arms ($10k+).
2. **No published work treats intervention logs from scripted/fiducial-guided laboratory arms as training data** for learned recovery policies, nor compares scripted, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over extended campaigns.
3. **No published robotics paper combines confidence sequences, change-point detection, and pre-registration** for a reliability campaign with a deliberately improved controller. The statistical components exist individually in reliability engineering and clinical trial methodology but have not been assembled for this use case.

However, the supplied pages do not state whether California’s official metrics are expressed as disengagements per mile, miles per disengagement/intervention, or another normalized measure, nor do they reproduce the DMV’s reporting fields or standards.
contexts.question: How is "disengagement" defined for autonomous vehicles, what metrics are used (disengagements per mile, miles between interventions), and what reporting standards exist for California DMV?

contexts.context: The excerpt characterizes an autonomous-vehicle disengagement as an event classified according to who or what initiates the intervention: automated disengagements are initiated by the AV, manual disengagements by the test operator, and planned disengagements by a pre-programmed error occurrence. It reports that prior research commonly examines cumulative disengagement frequency in relation to cumulative mileage and finds a positive correlation as vehicles accumulate miles. However, the excerpt does not provide a formal mathematical definition of disengagements per mile or miles between interventions, nor does it state a specific conversion or reporting formula for either metric. For California, the CA DMV database is presented as the principal source for manufacturer performance, mileage, and disengagement trends, while DMV reports provide detailed AV incident information. The excerpt also notes an important limitation: the CA DMV does not supply predefined classifications for the causes of disengagements, so researchers adopt categories from prior studies. The discussed study uses aggregated and classified disengagement and mileage data and justifies Pearson correlation for examining their linear relationship. Thus, the passage supports the general measurement context and data source, but additional sections or DMV regulations would be needed for the official reporting standard, required fields, definitions, and precise calculation of rates or miles between interventions.

contexts.context: The excerpt treats a disengagement as a manual intervention that separates autonomous-driving and manual-driving segments, or as a system re-enable event. In the described signal representation, autonomous and manual periods are identified over time, with an intervention or system re-enable signal marking the transition. The paper argues that raw disengagement counts are insufficient unless normalized by exposure: distance driven, operating time, testing location, and the number of vehicles involved. Accordingly, useful comparison metrics include disengagements per mile (or per unit of autonomous distance) and its reciprocal, miles between interventions; however, the supplied pages do not provide the formal equations or exact definitions for those metrics. The authors propose intervention maps and additional spatiotemporal metrics, including separating results by road type and accounting for safety-driver dependability, to enable less biased comparisons. For California reporting, the excerpt states that the DMV requires entities testing on public roads to submit annual summaries of disengagements. It notes that many reports provide annual counts but are generally not time- or distance-normalized, making comparisons of safety and robustness difficult. The excerpt also says that, at the time of writing, California had 66 entities with valid testing permits and three with driverless testing permits.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a formal definition of “disengagement” or describe California DMV reporting standards. It treats disengagement as an event requiring a driver- or system-initiated intervention or takeover, and analyzes it using exposure-normalized measures rather than raw event totals. The principal metric is disengagement frequency per 1000 km (equivalent in concept to disengagements per mile), which is used to compare years and operators. The inverse metric is distance traveled per disengagement, described as the distance before a takeover or intervention; this can be expressed as kilometers per disengagement or miles between interventions. The article emphasizes that raw annual disengagement counts can be misleading because they are affected by mileage, fleet size, operating environments, software updates, and outliers. For Waymo, the normalized rate declined from 0.12 to 0.04 disengagements per 1000 km between 2018 and 2022, while the distance-to-disengagement ratio increased over time. However, the authors caution that improvements cannot be attributed solely to technological progress because operators’ institutional policies for identifying and reporting disengagements are unknown. Thus, the excerpt supports discussion of the metrics and reporting comparability, but not specific California DMV definitions or requirements.

contexts.context: The excerpt defines an autonomous-vehicle disengagement under California Code of Regulations § 227.38 as deactivation of autonomous mode after an autonomous-technology failure is detected or when safe operation requires the test driver to take immediate manual control. For driverless vehicles, disengagement occurs when vehicle, occupant, or public safety requires the autonomous technology to be deactivated. The reported causes can include autonomous-system anomalies, operational-design-domain (ODD) exits, safety-driver intervention, driver discretion, consideration of other road users, and ADS software limitations or errors. The excerpt indicates that California DMV reporting includes annual reports describing disengagement frequency, but it does not provide a specific formula or numerical threshold for disengagements per mile or miles between interventions. California testing-permit holders must submit the Monthly Report of Autonomous Vehicle Disengagements, form OL 311R, by the tenth day of each month, beginning 30 days after permit issuance. The report covers every disengagement and records metadata such as VIN, software version, GPS coordinates, initiator, cause categories, and post-event actions. Separate collision reports are required within ten days, and hard-braking events above 0.5 g are reported monthly. Noncompliance can result in information requests, permit suspension, or revocation.
contexts.question: How is "disengagement" defined for autonomous vehicles, what metrics are used (disengagements per mile, miles between interventions), and what reporting standards exist for California DMV?

contexts.context: The excerpt presents Fleet-DAgger as a family of Interactive Fleet Learning (IFL) algorithms for allocating limited human supervision across many robots while the shared robot policy continually learns from human interventions. The setting involves a fleet of independent robots, typically far more robots than supervisors, with a robot-gated allocation policy deciding which robots receive assistance. Fleet-DAgger addresses the supervisor-allocation problem, where allocation influences human burden, task performance, and learning efficiency. Return on Human Effort (ROHE) is introduced as a new metric for evaluating IFL algorithms, but the excerpted pages do not provide its formal mathematical definition; they only establish that it measures the benefit or performance obtained relative to human supervisory effort. The reported evaluation compares a novel Fleet-DAgger method against four baselines using 100 simulated robots. The paper also reports a physical block-pushing experiment involving four ABB YuMi robot arms and two remote human supervisors. Across the reported experiments, allocation of humans to robots substantially affects fleet performance, and the novel Fleet-DAgger method achieves up to 8.8 times higher ROHE than the baselines.

contexts.context: The excerpt defines Fleet-DAgger as a family of interactive fleet-learning algorithms for multi-robot, multi-human supervision. Each algorithm specifies a supervisor-allocation policy that assigns a limited set of human supervisors to robots, using a priority function based on each robot’s state and the current robot policy. The learning component is interactive imitation learning with dataset aggregation: human teleoperation data are added to the accumulated dataset and used to update the robot policy through supervised learning. Allocation rules preserve ongoing hard resets and teleoperation for minimum durations to reduce thrashing, then assign available humans to the highest-priority unassisted robots. The excerpt defines Return on Human Effort (ROHE) as the expected cumulative fleet reward divided by total human assistance time, with normalization by the numbers of robots and supervisors and an added one in the denominator for the zero-assistance case. The broader setting involves N robots and M much smaller than N human supervisors, with each human helping at most one robot at a time. Although the question asks about achieved results with robot fleets and human supervisors, these pages provide the problem formulation and algorithm descriptions only; they do not report empirical outcomes, fleet sizes used in experiments, or comparative performance results. contexts.context: Fleet-DAgger is presented as a family of interactive fleet-learning algorithms for allocating a limited number of human supervisors among a larger fleet of robots. It uses interactive imitation learning with Dataset Aggregation (DAgger): human teleoperation produces additional online demonstrations, these are added to the dataset of all human data collected so far, and supervised learning updates the shared robot policy. The distinctive component is a supervisor-allocation policy based on a priority function that scores each robot using its current state and the current robot policy; robots with higher scores receive attention first. A minimum teleoperation duration is also specified to reduce thrashing, while ongoing hard resets and required interventions continue until completed. The Return on Human Effort (ROHE) objective is the expected cumulative reward of the entire fleet divided by total human assistance time, with a scaling factor involving the fleet and supervisor counts and an added one in the denominator for the zero-human-time case. It therefore evaluates fleet performance per unit of human effort. The supplied excerpt establishes the multi-robot, multi-human formulation and Fleet-DAgger mechanism, but it ends before reporting experimental findings; consequently, specific results for fleet sizes, numbers of human supervisors, or comparative performance are not available here.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Sirius as a human-in-the-loop framework for deploying partially autonomous robots. The robot handles decisions in situations where its policy is reliable, while a human operator monitors execution and takes over during difficult or potentially failing situations. This division of labor is intended to provide safe, consistently successful task execution while allowing the robot to improve over time and reduce human workload. Sirius learns from deployment data by estimating human trust from intervention behavior and assigning different weights to training samples. In the intervention-weighted behavioral-cloning procedure, robot actions immediately preceding a human intervention are treated as low-quality data because the human judged that failure was likely, whereas human demonstrations and takeover interventions are treated as high-quality data. The policy is then trained with weighted behavioral cloning, reinforcing trusted behavior while avoiding imitation of actions associated with failure. The excerpt reports aggregate performance improvements—an 8% policy-success-rate boost in simulation and 27% on real hardware, with twice-faster convergence and 85% memory reduction—but it does not provide the specific intervention rates, task-by-task success rates, or robot-arm platforms used. Those details would require later pages or supplementary material.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes SIRIUS-FLEET as a multi-task interactive robot fleet-learning framework for improving robot behavior during deployment. It combines a continually fine-tuned multi-task policy with runtime monitoring based on a visual world model. The world model is pretrained on diverse robot trajectories and predicts future latent states or task outcomes from past visual observations. Its shared representations support two anomaly predictors: failure prediction, which identifies failures resembling previously observed human-labeled failures, and out-of-distribution prediction, which detects novel or unfamiliar situations. When an anomaly is predicted, the system requests human intervention; deployment data and human feedback are then used to update the policy and monitoring criteria. The framework adapts its anomaly thresholds as robot autonomy improves, with the stated goal of reducing human workload over time. The excerpt identifies evaluations in RoboCasa simulation and Mutex in the real world. contexts.context: The excerpt describes Sirius as a human-in-the-loop deployment and learning framework in which the robot autonomously executes long-horizon manipulation tasks while a human supervises. If the human observes undesirable behavior, such as a gear becoming stuck, they intervene through a 6-DoF SpaceMouse, directly controlling the robot; once the robot is again in an acceptable state, control is returned to the autonomous policy. Sirius is evaluated on contact-rich manipulation tasks, including simulated nut assembly and tool hanging, and real-world gear insertion and coffee-pod packing, using a Franka Emika Panda arm with a parallel-jaw gripper. The learning setup uses an intervention-guided weighting scheme, with the target intervention probability set to P*(intv) = 1/2, or 50%; the text says this value increases the intervention weight to a reasonable level and is examined in an ablation study. The excerpt does not define intervention-weighted behavior cloning in full or report measured intervention rates and task success rates. It also does not mention any robot arms other than the Franka Emika Panda in the supplied passage. Baselines include IWR, BC-RNN, and IQL.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Sirius as a continual human-in-the-loop learning framework for robot manipulation. Its goal is to use deployment experience and human corrective feedback to improve the robot policy, increase autonomy, and reduce the human operator’s workload. Sirius has two simultaneous processes: Robot Deployment, in which the robot executes tasks while a human monitors and intervenes when necessary, and Policy Update, in which deployment data are used to train the policy for subsequent task-execution rounds. The system begins with an initial policy trained from a small number of human demonstrations; the memory buffer stores demonstration and later deployment trajectories, including states, actions, rewards, and data-class labels. The excerpt also introduces weighted behavioral cloning, where each state-action example’s log-likelihood is multiplied by a weight. It identifies Intervention-weighted Regression (IWR) as a human-in-the-loop weighted behavioral-cloning method, but the provided text ends before explaining IWR’s weighting rule. The excerpt does not report the measured intervention rates, task success rates, or the robot-arm platforms on which they were evaluated. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Sirius as a framework for human-in-the-loop robot manipulation and learning during deployment. Its key mechanism is intervention-based reweighting, which is intended to extract common principles of human–robot interaction while reducing sensitivity to differences among human operators. The study reports substantial variation in performance when learning from individual human intervention datasets: policy success rates range from 44.8% to 72.7%. Intervention involvement is quantified using the Intervention Sample Ratio, defined as the fraction of timesteps completed by humans relative to total trajectory timesteps. Across the intervention dataset, the mean intervention sample ratio was 0.32, with a standard deviation of 0.11, a maximum of 0.57, and a minimum of 0.19. The excerpt also reports an average intervention length of 15.28 timesteps and an average of 2.80 interventions per trajectory, though these are not intervention rates. The provided pages do not specify the robot arm or arms used in the experiments, nor do they fully define intervention-weighted behavior cloning beyond describing Sirius’s intervention-based reweighting scheme. contexts.context: The excerpt describes SIRIUS-FLEET as a multi-task interactive robot fleet-learning framework that combines a multi-task policy with runtime monitoring. It uses a visual world model and task-adaptive anomaly predictors, including failure and out-of-distribution prediction, to identify problematic executions and trigger timely human intervention. The baseline comparison used five RoboCasa tasks from different categories and compared SIRIUS-FLEET with MoMart, PATO, and ThriftyDAgger; SIRIUS-FLEET outperformed them in combined policy performance and ROHE. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies HIL-SERL as a human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning system for precise and dexterous robotic manipulation. During autonomous rollouts, a human operator can intervene at any timestep and take control for up to N steps, applying corrective actions when the policy is failing or exploring inefficiently. Intervention transitions are stored in both demonstration and reinforcement-learning buffers, while policy transitions before and after interventions are stored only in the RL buffer. The system uses RLPD, sparse binary task-completion rewards, and a separate DQN-based critic for discrete gripper actions. contexts.context: HIL-SERL (Human-in-the-Loop Soft Actor-Critic with Reinforcement Learning, as identified by the article title) is a human-in-the-loop robotic manipulation approach that uses human corrections to optimize a policy with task-specific reinforcement-learning rewards, rather than using corrections only for supervised imitation learning. In the reported experiments, the main measurements were task success rate, cycle time, intervention rate, and the number of human interventions over training. HIL-SERL’s success rate rose rapidly to 100%, while intervention rates and cycle times decreased; the intervention rate ultimately reached 0%, indicating autonomous execution. Across nearly all tasks, it reached 100% success after approximately 1–2.5 hours of real-world training. The comparison HG-DAgger baseline averaged 49.7% success, with fluctuating success, no consistent decline in intervention rate, and no cycle-time improvement. The figure shows running-average curves over 20 episodes for RAM insertion, USB grasp-insert, IKEA top-panel assembly, and car-dashboard tasks, but this excerpt does not provide exact intervention counts or numerical intervention-rate values for each task. contexts.context: HIL-SERL stands for Human-in-the-Loop Sample-Efficient Robotic Reinforcement Learning. It is a vision-based real-world reinforcement-learning system that combines a pretrained visual backbone, a sample-efficient off-policy algorithm based on RLPD, human demonstrations and corrections, and a safety-oriented low-level controller. The tasks included dynamic manipulation, precision assembly, object handover, Jenga-block extraction, and complex assembly, performed with either one or two robotic arms. contexts.context: LabRobFail is a failure-centric framework and benchmark for analyzing robotic failures in chemical self-driving laboratories. Its data-generation component, LabRobFail-Sim, automatically injects controllable failures at control, physics, and semantic levels, producing LabRobFail-Data with more than 20,000 operation trajectories, over 70 task scenarios, five major failure categories, and 11 fine-grained failure types. LabRobFail-Bench evaluates six capabilities: task understanding, failure detection, temporal localization, severity assessment, failure classification, and actionable/fine-grained correction. Failures for laboratory robot arms are coded using category abbreviations: Perception Failure (PF), Grasping Failure (GF), Motion Failure (MF), Logic Failure (LF), and Safety Failure (SF). The examples shown assign planning collision to PF, object dropped to GF, incomplete opening to MF, sequence error to LF, and protocol violation to SF. Thus, the coding scheme links an observed or injected arm failure to a broad causal category and a finer-grained failure type, supporting localization, diagnosis, severity judgment, and recovery-action evaluation.

It includes LabRobFail-Sim, a simulation platform with automated, controllable failure injection; LabRobFail-Data, a large-scale dataset; and LabRobFail-Bench, a multidimensional benchmark. The taxonomy defines five major categories—Perception, Grasping, Motion, Logic, and Safety—with 11 fine-grained failure types. The dataset spans more than 70 task instances, from short manipulations to long-horizon workflows, and contains over 20,000 operation trajectories balancing successful and failed executions. The benchmark evaluates whether a system can detect a failure, localize it temporally, classify its failure mode, assess severity, and generate fine-grained corrective guidance. Failures for laboratory robot arms are coded/generated through perturbations at three levels: control-level corruption of poses and gripper commands; physics-level changes to dynamics such as friction, mass, and viscosity to model slippage or grasp instability; and semantic-level changes such as reversing or skipping task steps and substituting target objects or reagents. These perturbations produce labeled trajectories for training and evaluation, while LabRobFail-VLM represents diagnoses as structured predictions over failure presence, localization, type, severity, and corrective guidance.

LabRobFail-Data organizes failures into five major categories: Safety, Logic, Motion, Grasping, and Perception, with eleven fine-grained types. Failures are represented using sequential keyframe grids: rows correspond to different camera viewpoints and columns to later time steps, allowing the robot arm’s motion and the point of failure to be examined spatiotemporally. An LLM selects questions and answers them from visual observations and metadata, while fixed categories are used for selected dimensions. Corrections are encoded as executable instructions using four fields: position adjustment, orientation adjustment, gripper state, and execution condition. contexts.context: The excerpt reports that increasing network latency degrades teleoperation performance overall, including the study’s recorded task metrics. Relevant delays range from roughly 100 ms for Earth–LEO communication to several hundred milliseconds for other Earth-orbit and lunar relay scenarios. As latency increases, operators must predict robot outcomes further in advance, while delayed or out-of-sync feedback makes it harder to adjust actions accurately; errors and uncertainty therefore increase. Operators commonly respond with a “move-and-wait” strategy, inserting stationary pauses to check or re-baseline their predictions. This behavior substantially increases task completion time and is described as reflecting reduced trust in the delayed system. The excerpt does not provide numerical effect sizes specifically for tens-to-hundreds-of-milliseconds latency, nor does it report a distinct metric called “demonstration quality.” It also does not quantify error rates or completion-time changes by latency level; it only states the direction of the effects. The broader study tested latency up to 2.6 seconds and found that increased latency reduced all recorded performance metrics, but the supplied pages do not give detailed results for the requested latency range.

The investigated system was a remotely controlled four-degree-of-freedom ultrasound robot connected over WLAN/Wi-Fi, with network speeds ranging from 0.72 to 2.42 Mbps. Position error was assessed using predefined paths that varied in length, direction, and number of direction changes, while only one degree of freedom was operated at a time. The article frames delay, jitter, and packet loss as causes of undesired manipulator execution and potentially reduced motion accuracy, but the provided pages contain experimental methods rather than measured latency-dependent outcomes. contexts.context: The excerpt reports a human-subjects study of delay in an arm-scale mimicry-control teleoperation system, in which users’ six-degree-of-freedom hand movements were mapped directly to a robot end effector. It distinguishes onset latency—the interval between issuing a command and the robot beginning to execute it—from robot slowness, in which the robot moves more slowly than the operator. The study found that delays negatively affect teleoperation task performance, but that their effects depend on delay type rather than simply delay magnitude. Participants quickly adapted to robot slowness by adopting alternate motor strategies, whereas no comparable strategy emerged for significant onset latency. Movement-path analysis revealed these adaptation differences in addition to task-level performance effects. The supplied pages do not provide numerical results for latency in the tens-to-hundreds of milliseconds range, nor do they report specific changes in error rate, task-completion time, or demonstration quality. They do indicate that the evaluation involved tracing cursive letters and analyzing the robot end-effector path, which may serve as task-performance and movement-quality measures. Thus, the excerpt supports a qualitative conclusion that onset latency impairs performance and is difficult to compensate for, while slower robot execution can be accommodated, but it does not contain the requested quantitative measurements.

contexts.context: RaC (Recovery and Correction) is an iterative imitation-learning data-collection strategy that combines human-provided recovery segments with corrective segments and full expert demonstrations. Recovery segments start from failures or out-of-distribution states and return the robot to familiar, in-distribution states encountered earlier in demonstrations; corrective segments directly advance or complete the current subtask. The central idea is that recovery is often easier to learn than precise task completion, allowing the robot to reset, retry, and reduce the effects of compounding errors. The protocol begins with an initial round of full demonstrations, trains a policy, then repeatedly collects human interventions during rollouts of the current policy, adds the intervention data to the dataset, and retrains. The robot platform uses two 7-degree-of-freedom xArm-7 manipulators with scaled-down soft grippers, supported by overhead and wrist RGB cameras and 60-Hz reactive control. This excerpt does not report numerical intervention rates or task success rates; those figures would need to be obtained from other sections of the paper. It does establish that RaC is intended to improve the scaling slope of task success versus data size by explicitly increasing recovery and correction data.

contexts.context: The excerpt characterizes RaC (Recovery and Correction) as an imitation-learning approach for long-horizon robot tasks that explicitly trains both recovery and corrective behavior. Recovery returns the robot from a failure or out-of-distribution state to a familiar in-distribution state, while correction attempts to advance the current sub-task. This supports a recovery-then-retry strategy: the policy can make progress on an initial attempt, reset after failure, and retry, with repeated attempts increasing the probability of success. RaC’s intervention-data protocol requires each human intervention to contain a recovery segment followed by a correction segment, ensuring a balanced mixture rather than data dominated by corrections. The episode is terminated after the intervention so later sub-tasks are not trained on states produced by a mixed human-policy distribution; this also concentrates the data-collection budget on earlier sub-tasks. contexts.context: The excerpt describes RaC as a human-intervention data-collection and imitation-learning approach that deliberately pairs recovery behavior—getting the robot back on track after failure—with corrective behavior. Its objective is to help policies mitigate compounding errors, retry failed actions, and perform better on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks. The protocol uses two rules: interventions follow a recover-then-correct structure, and the episode is terminated after the intervention ends rather than allowing the policy to continue. This is intended to keep the collected trajectory cleanly representative of recovery–correction behavior and avoid contaminating later data with mixed human/policy states. contexts.context: The excerpt describes Genie Centurion (GCENT) as a real-robot training and supervision system centered on targeted human intervention rather than continuous shared control. It uses VR controllers to operate a dual-arm AgiBot G01 robot, with explicit modes for inference, intervention, rewind, and awaiting intervention. A human can rewind the robot to an earlier state and provide a corrective demonstration at a failure point, after which the corrected trajectory is added to the training data. The system’s Task Sentinel is a reward-model-style value-predictor head, fine-tuned from InternVL2.5-2B, that independently determines whether each task step has succeeded and can run alongside the policy on real robots. Sentinel-triggered “Awaiting Intervention” states and automatically recorded mode labels help identify high-quality corrective samples. The data loop repeatedly deploys, monitors, rewinds or corrects, aggregates data, and retrains the policy and Sentinel, with the stated objective of reducing intervention rates while increasing success rates. However, these pages do not provide quantitative success-rate results, a measured data-yield-to-human-effort ratio, or specific evidence about one human supervising many robots; they only indicate that prior multi-robot supervision work exists and that GCENT aims at scalable, targeted data collection.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Genie Centurion (GCENT) as a real-robot training and supervision framework designed to improve data yield relative to human effort. Its Task Sentinel is a multimodal model that monitors image observations and task instructions, detects whether an atomic step has been completed, and automatically advances when successful. If a step remains incomplete beyond a predefined timeout, it places the robot in “Awaiting Intervention” and requests human help. In Human-Gated mode, the operator intervenes when errors occur; as policy performance improves, Sentinel allows one operator to supervise multiple robots and request assistance only when necessary. When intervention is needed, the operator can rewind up to three seconds using the robot’s state buffer, apply physical corrections, and provide a targeted demonstration. The policy is trained only on these human intervention segments, concentrating supervision on corrective, high-value data rather than complete passive trajectories. Across four real-world tasks—sandwich assembly, connector insertion, microwave heating, and typing—GCENT achieved an average final score of 0.93, compared with 0.38 for passive collection and 0.53 for adversarial collection under the reported evaluation. The paper reports a 55% improvement over passive methods and 40% over ADC with equal data budgets, with all tasks exceeding 0.9 within 3–5 GCENT rounds. A precise numerical human-hours-per-success or yield-to-effort ratio is not provided in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Genie Centurion (GCENT) as a real-robot training framework designed to support one-human-to-many-robot supervision. Its Task Sentinel autonomously detects potential failures and requests human intervention, reducing the need for continuous monitoring. In a one-human-two-robot sandwich-assembly experiment, collection efficiency—defined using effective frames after subtracting paused waiting frames and normalized against single-robot operation—was 1.86 at a 40% model success rate, 1.90 at 60%, and 1.92 at 80%. Intervention rates simultaneously fell from 47% to 39% and 27%, respectively, showing improved supervision efficiency as policies became more capable. GCENT achieved an average final task score of 0.93, reported as a 55% improvement over passive collection and 40% over adversarial collection under identical data budgets. It reached scores above 0.9 within three to five rounds, while requiring only 44.5% of the frames used by alternative methods to reach comparable performance. The paper concludes that declining intervention frequency and higher collection efficiency establish a foundation for scalable single-operator N-robot deployment.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Fleet-DAgger, a framework for allocating one or more human supervisors across a robot fleet. At each timestep, robots receive priority scores; an available human is assigned to the highest-priority currently unassisted robot, while minimum intervention times prevent thrashing. The text defines several allocation strategies, including Constraint, uncertainty-based, goal-risk-based, and the proposed Constraint-Uncertainty-Risk (C.U.R.) method. It also introduces the Interactive Fleet Learning Benchmark (IFLB), which evaluates fleet learning using cumulative successful task completions, cumulative hard resets, cumulative idle time, and return on human effort (ROHE). The benchmark supports Humanoid, ANYmal, and AllegroHand environments in NVIDIA Isaac Gym and is designed to simulate hundreds of learning robots efficiently on a single GPU. However, this excerpt does not mention Genie Centurion, Task Sentinel, real-robot experiments, specific success-rate results, or a data-yield-to-effort ratio beyond the general ROHE metric.
